tecnicas.observacao: Poda (compressão) do prompt few-shot: atenção do CodeBERT (janela de 500 tokens) dá o valor de cada token e uma mochila 0-1 escolhe os tokens dentro do limite de entrada do GPT-3.5-turbo (4096 tokens), o que abre espaço para mais exemplos de classes do ClassEval (em média 4 exemplos, segundo a Seção 4.4). O prompt herda do prompt base a persona/instrução ('You are an expert programmer'; 'Below is an instruction...') → instrucao; os exemplos resolvidos de classes (esqueleto + solução) → exemplos e contexto (código fornecido como demonstração); o esqueleto da classe-alvo fornecido como insumo → contexto. A compressão por seleção de tokens foi classificada como 'outro' (compressão do prompt guiada por atenção); não há busca do prompt guiada por desempenho. Em relação ao prompt base (Few-shot Without Pruning), acrescenta a poda ('outro') e aumenta o número de exemplos (de 1 para, em média, 4), o que fica dentro das categorias já presentes. O isolamento por ingrediente vem da ablação 'Random Pruning' (Seção 5.2), que segue a mesma implementação mas remove tokens ao acaso; o estudo não informa explicitamente o número de exemplos na condição de poda aleatória. Contra 'Few-shot Without Pruning' o contraste é de pacote (poda + mais exemplos), sem isolamento de cada parte.

citacoes.trecho: We propose an attention-guided pruning strategy that selectively removes less informative code tokens, allowing more representative examples to be included in the prompt and thus providing richer semantic context for LLMs.

Experiments on the ClassEval dataset using GPT-3.5 demonstrate that our strategy significantly outperforms random pruning, achieving 4.2%, 10.2%, and 13% higher accuracy in class-level code generation.
Further analysis shows that pruning up to 40% of tokens while including four additional examples maximizes LLM performance, enabling more accurate and coherent class-level code generation.

citacoes.trecho: Certainly, these examples do not contain desired code snippet and are chosen randomly.
The second process is to request LLM with temperature of 0 for the stability of LLM's output, namely GPT-3.5-turbo, to generate the code solution snippet for each input processed prompt.
The time complexity of attention-guided pruning algorithm is O(N∗L_T), where L_T denotes the target numbers of tokens.
Additionally, the 0-1 backpack algorithm demands to handle two-dimensional array when programming dynamically, costing space in memory.
The first experiment we conduct, compared with the pruning strategy we propose, is few-shot learning of LLM without pruning.
Furthermore, the prompt includes only a single code generation example in its examples part.
The second baseline experiment is conducted for ablation study, named random pruning.
In our work, we take all 100 class-level code generation tasks in ClassEval into experiments.
In addition, the desired code snippet does not emerge in those examples, chosen stochastically, in the prompt.

With several tries of pruning tokens from prompt, we find that pruning over 40% tokens can destroy both semantics and structure of prompt and the prompt just contains some meaningless and unrelated tokens.
Therefore the the pruning strategy is tested with the set of prune percentages: 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% which averagely supply 4 code generation examples to the prompt.
For each method we test, we adopt greedy sampling to generate 2 code samples and evaluate the performance of each method by Pass@k with k = {1, 3, 5}.
For the attention-based pruning strategy, we used the CodeBERT model with default parameters to generate specific attention values and set the window length to 500 tokens.
To save on training time and costs, each code generation task requested the GPT model twice.
However, the LLM performs inferior when the pruning percentage of input prompt augments to 40% with the only Pass@k of Class-level and Method-level, 3.4% and 10.4% respectively.

Taking advantage of the context and focusing on the fine-grained token-level adjustment demonstrates that attention-guided pruning is significantly better than random pruning for both class-level and well-studied method-level code.
